output.brief: The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: only 32% of them had the 18 months in level the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28% vs 29%), approval rates (71% vs 74%) and promotion rates (20% vs 21%) are nearly the same. Adjusting for eligibility gives an expected remote rate of 8.2% against the observed 7.6%. Remote staff do not leave more often. I can't confirm the proximity bias the COO described. The eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. Stretch-assignment access is untested; managers' comments hint at it. Don't adopt the three-day office rule. It would be built on a diagnosis the data don't support, and it would hit about 180 people hired on home-based contracts. Instead, hold the proposal and report promotion rates for eligible staff only. Re-check at FY2027, and collect staffing data on stretch work meanwhile. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding and moderate on the residual question of bias.
